The Wigner–Eckart theorem splits every matrix element of a tensor operator into two factors: a Clebsch–Gordan coefficient, which is pure geometry, and a reduced matrix element, which carries all of the physics. The previous memo proved this with a construction. Apply the operator to one irrep, recombine the results with Clebsch–Gordan coefficients into “tilde” states ∣J,M~⟩,\lvert\widetilde{J,M}\rangle\text{,}∣J,M​⟩, and read off the reduced matrix elements as the coefficients of the tilde states in the original basis.

This memo carries out that construction in full, in the smallest space where it has any teeth: three spin-12\h21​ particles, with the spin of particle 2 as the tensor operator. The space is only eight-dimensional, so every state can be written out in the up/down basis, and every claim can be checked by hand. And spin 12\h21​ occurs twice, so the reduced matrix elements need labels that say which copy we start in and which copy we land in. Along the way we’ll meet a puzzle (twelve states in an eight-dimensional space) and a tower of states that is identically zero.

3Two ways to use the operator

Pick one of the three irreps: (12,α=1),(\h,\alpha{=}1)\text{,}(21​,α=1), (12,α=2),(\h,\alpha{=}2)\text{,}(21​,α=2), or (32).(\tth)\text{.}(23​). There are two natural ways to make new states out of it.

Route 1: product states. Apply all three of the Sl1\Sl{l}Sl1​ to all the states of the irrep. For the (12,α=2)(\h,\alpha{=}2)(21​,α=2) irrep this gives six states:

S+11∣12,12,α=2⟩,S01∣12,12,α=2⟩,S−11∣12,12,α=2⟩,S+11∣12,−12,α=2⟩,S01∣12,−12,α=2⟩,S−11∣12,−12,α=2⟩.\begin{gathered} \Sl{+1}\ka{\h}{2},\quad \Sl{0}\ka{\h}{2},\quad \Sl{-1}\ka{\h}{2},\\ \Sl{+1}\ka{\mh}{2},\quad \Sl{0}\ka{\mh}{2},\quad \Sl{-1}\ka{\mh}{2}. \end{gathered}S+11​∣21​,21​,α=2⟩,S01​∣21​,21​,α=2⟩,S−11​∣21​,21​,α=2⟩,S+11​∣21​,−21​,α=2⟩,S01​∣21​,−21​,α=2⟩,S−11​∣21​,−21​,α=2⟩.​
(5)

We’ll call these the product states. Why “product”? Because Sl1∣12,m⟩\Sl{l}\ket{\h,m}Sl1​∣21​,m⟩ behaves exactly like the product state ∣1,l⟩∣12,m⟩.\ket{1,l}\ket{\h,m}\text{.}∣1,l⟩∣21​,m⟩. Precisely, the correspondence ∣1,l⟩∣12,m⟩↦Sl1∣12,m,α=2⟩\ket{1,l}\ket{\h,m}\mapsto\Sl{l}\ka{m}{2}∣1,l⟩∣21​,m⟩↦Sl1​∣21​,m,α=2⟩ is linear and commutes with the Ja;J_a\text{;}Ja​; that’s what the commutator in eq. (3) says. So any identity built from linear combinations and the action of the JaJ_aJa​ carries over from the ∣1,l⟩∣12,m⟩\ket{1,l}\ket{\h,m}∣1,l⟩∣21​,m⟩ to the product states. That includes every Clebsch–Gordan expansion and every result of acting with J±.J_\pm\text{.}J±​.

What does not carry over is the inner product. The ∣1,l⟩∣12,m⟩\ket{1,l}\ket{\h,m}∣1,l⟩∣21​,m⟩ are orthonormal, so the six product states are orthonormal only symbolically, as abstract labels. As actual vectors in H1⊗H2⊗H3\mathcal H_1\otimes\mathcal H_2\otimes\mathcal H_3H1​⊗H2​⊗H3​ they need not be normalized or orthogonal, and some may even vanish. The only orthogonality we’re guaranteed in the actual space comes from J3J_3J3​ and J2:J^2\text{:}J2: states with different eigenvalues of these Hermitian operators are orthogonal.

4Twelve states in an eight-dimensional space

Whichever route we take, the new states live in H1⊗H2⊗H3.\mathcal H_1\otimes\mathcal H_2\otimes \mathcal H_3\text{.}H1​⊗H2​⊗H3​. So they can be expanded in the single-spin states ∣↑↑↑⟩,\ket{\U\U\U}\text{,}∣↑↑↑⟩, ∣↑↑↓⟩,\ket{\U\U\D}\text{,}∣↑↑↓⟩, …, or in the original basis {∣32,m⟩,∣12,m,α=1⟩,∣12,m,α=2⟩}.\{\ket{\tth,m},\ka{m}{1},\ka{m}{2}\}\text{.}{∣23​,m⟩,∣21​,m,α=1⟩,∣21​,m,α=2⟩}. For example, ∣12,12~⟩(2)\tk{\h}{\h}∣21​,21​​⟩(2) has to be made of ∣12,12,α=1⟩\ka{\h}{1}∣21​,21​,α=1⟩ and ∣12,12,α=2⟩,\ka{\h}{2}\text{,}∣21​,21​,α=2⟩, since nothing else in the space transforms the same way under the Ja.J_a\text{.}Ja​. So

∣12,12~⟩(2)=kα=2,β=1 ∣12,12,β=1⟩+kα=2,β=2 ∣12,12,β=2⟩,\tk{\h}{\h} = k_{\alpha=2,\beta=1}\,\kb{\h}{1} + k_{\alpha=2,\beta=2}\,\kb{\h}{2},∣21​,21​​⟩(2)=kα=2,β=1​∣21​,21​,β=1⟩+kα=2,β=2​∣21​,21​,β=2⟩,
(12)

where β\betaβ labels the copy of spin 12\h21​ that the state lands in. Finding the kαβk_{\alpha\beta}kαβ​ means expanding everything in single spins, and that is the job of Sections 6⁠–⁠8.

First, though, let’s count. Acting with S±1,01\Sl{\pm1,0}S±1,01​ on the (12,α=1)(\h,\alpha{=}1)(21​,α=1) irrep gives 6 states, on (12,α=2)(\h,\alpha{=}2)(21​,α=2) another 6, and on (32)(\tth)(23​) a full 12. Each set is orthonormal only symbolically. In the actual space none of the three sets is orthonormal in general, and states from different sets need not be orthogonal to each other either. All we can say is that within one set, the Route-2 states with different (J,M)(J,M)(J,M) are orthogonal or zero, since they have different eigenvalues of the Hermitian operators J2J^2J2 and J3.J_3\text{.}J3​.

But look at that last set. Acting on the (32)(\tth)(23​) irrep gives 12 states, and the whole space is only 8-dimensional! Is something wrong? No. The 12 states are orthonormal only symbolically, so there’s no contradiction: 12 vectors in an 8-dimensional space simply have to be linearly dependent.44 The pigeonhole principle, linear-algebra edition. Route 2 shows how. There the 12 states organize as 1⊗32=12⊕32⊕52,1\otimes\tth=\h\oplus\tth\oplus\fh\text{,}1⊗23​=21​⊕23​⊕25​, that is, 2+4+62+4+62+4+6 states (Fig. 3).Figure 3 The entire J~=52\widetilde J=\fhJ=25​ tower, 6 of the 12 states, is zero, because the space contains no spin 52\fh25​ for it to land in. (We’ll see this explicitly in Section 5.) The J~=32\widetilde J=\tthJ=23​ and J~=12\widetilde J=\hJ=21​ towers survive. In Route 1 the dependence is less tidy: only two of the product states vanish, S+11∣32,32⟩\Sl{+1}\ket{\tth,\tth}S+11​∣23​,23​⟩ and S−11∣32,−32⟩,\Sl{-1}\ket{\tth,\mtth}\text{,}S−11​∣23​,−23​⟩, but the 12 product states span only a 6-dimensional subspace.

5The spin-52\fh25​ tower is zero

Start from the top state,

∣52,52~⟩=S+11∣32,32⟩.\tq{\fh}{\fh} = \Sl{+1}\ket{\tth,\tth}.∣25​,25​​⟩=S+11​∣23​,23​⟩.
(13)

We know that ∣32,32⟩=∣↑↑↑⟩\ket{\tth,\tth}=\ket{\U\U\U}∣23​,23​⟩=∣↑↑↑⟩ and that S+11=−12S+(2).\Sl{+1} = -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}S^{(2)}_+\text{.}S+11​=−2​1​S+(2)​. So

S+11∣32,32⟩=−12 S+(2)∣↑↑↑⟩=0,\Sl{+1}\ket{\tth,\tth} = -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\,S^{(2)}_+\ket{\U\U\U} = 0 ,S+11​∣23​,23​⟩=−2​1​S+(2)​∣↑↑↑⟩=0,
(14)

since particle 2 is already up. The top state ∣52,52~⟩\tq{\fh}{\fh}∣25​,25​​⟩ is zero, and every lower state in the tower is obtained from it by applying J−,J_-\text{,}J−​, so they’re all zero too.

But now we have a problem. How do we find ∣32,32~⟩,\tq{\tth}{\tth}\text{,}∣23​,23​​⟩, the top of the next tower? In Section 3 we got it by orthogonality to the state above it, and we can’t Gram–Schmidt against a vector that is zero!

The way out is to remember that the construction is symbolic. Nothing stops us from applying J−J_-J−​ to S+11∣32,32⟩\Sl{+1}\ket{\tth,\tth}S+11​∣23​,23​⟩ and working out the result as a combination of product states. Only when we expand that combination in the original basis do we find that it vanishes. Doing this,

and the left side is just ∣12,−12~⟩(2),\tk{\h}{\mh}\text{,}∣21​,−21​​⟩(2), since C−(12,12)=1.C^-(\h,\h)=1\text{.}C−(21​,21​)=1. In summary, the six tilde states are

S+11∣12,12,α=2⟩=112 ∣↑↑↑⟩,S01∣12,12,α=2⟩=16(12∣↑↓↑⟩−12∣↓↑↑⟩+∣↑↑↓⟩),S−11∣12,12,α=2⟩=112(2∣↑↓↓⟩−∣↓↓↑⟩),S+11∣12,−12,α=2⟩=−112(∣↑↑↓⟩−2∣↓↑↑⟩),S01∣12,−12,α=2⟩=16(−12∣↑↓↓⟩+12∣↓↑↓⟩+∣↓↓↑⟩),S−11∣12,−12,α=2⟩=112 ∣↓↓↓⟩.\begin{aligned} \Sl{+1}\ka{\h}{2} &= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{12}}\,\ket{\U\U\U},\\ \Sl{0}\ka{\h}{2} &= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}\Big(\tfrac12\ket{\U\D\U}-\tfrac12\ket{\D\U\U}+\ket{\U\U\D}\Big),\\ \Sl{-1}\ka{\h}{2} &= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{12}}\Big(2\ket{\U\D\D}-\ket{\D\D\U}\Big),\\[4pt] \Sl{+1}\ka{\mh}{2} &= -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{12}}\Big(\ket{\U\U\D}-2\ket{\D\U\U}\Big),\\ \Sl{0}\ka{\mh}{2} &= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}\Big(-\tfrac12\ket{\U\D\D}+\tfrac12\ket{\D\U\D}+\ket{\D\D\U}\Big),\\ \Sl{-1}\ka{\mh}{2} &= \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{12}}\,\ket{\D\D\D}. \end{aligned}S+11​∣21​,21​,α=2⟩S01​∣21​,21​,α=2⟩S−11​∣21​,21​,α=2⟩S+11​∣21​,−21​,α=2⟩S01​∣21​,−21​,α=2⟩S−11​∣21​,−21​,α=2⟩​=12​1​∣↑↑↑⟩,=6​1​(21​∣↑↓↑⟩−21​∣↓↑↑⟩+∣↑↑↓⟩),=12​1​(2∣↑↓↓⟩−∣↓↓↑⟩),=−12​1​(∣↑↑↓⟩−2∣↓↑↑⟩),=6​1​(−21​∣↑↓↓⟩+21​∣↓↑↓⟩+∣↓↓↑⟩),=12​1​∣↓↓↓⟩.​

For example, in the first line only the −∣↑↓↑⟩-\ket{\U\D\U}−∣↑↓↑⟩ term of ∣12,12,α=2⟩\ka{\h}{2}∣21​,21​,α=2⟩ has particle 2 down, so it’s the only one that survives S+(2),S^{(2)}_+\text{,}S+(2)​, and the coefficient is −12⋅16⋅(−1)=112.{-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}\cdot(-1)} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{12}}\text{.}−2​1​⋅6​1​⋅(−1)=12​1​.

Note that the tilde states are not unit vectors:

∥∣32,M~⟩(2)∥2=112,∥∣12,M~⟩(2)∥2=(12)2+(13)2=712.\big\lVert\tk{\tth}{M}\big\rVert^2 = \tfrac1{12},\qquad \big\lVert\tk{\h}{M}\big\rVert^2 = \big(\tfrac12\big)^2+\big(\tfrac1{\sqrt3}\big)^2 = \tfrac{7}{12}.​∣23​,M​⟩(2)​2=121​,​∣21​,M​⟩(2)​2=(21​)2+(3​1​)2=127​.

A check on the norms. Here’s a way to test eq. (42) without redoing any algebra. The spherical components satisfy ∑l(Sl1)†Sl1=(S1(2))2+(S2(2))2+(S3(2))2=34,\sum_l \big(\Sl{l}\big)^{\dagger}\Sl{l} =(S_1^{(2)})^2+(S_2^{(2)})^2+(S_3^{(2)})^2 = \tfrac34\text{,}∑l​(Sl1​)†Sl1​=(S1(2)​)2+(S2(2)​)2+(S3(2)​)2=43​, the squared spin of particle 2, so ∑l∥Sl1∣12,12,α=2⟩∥2=34.\sum_l\big\lVert\Sl{l}\ka{\h}{2}\big\rVert^2 = \tfrac34\text{.}∑l​​Sl1​∣21​,21​,α=2⟩​2=43​. (Indeed, the squared norms we found above add up to 112+14+512=34.){\tfrac1{12}+\tfrac14+\tfrac5{12}}=\tfrac34\text{.)}121​+41​+125​=43​.) On the other hand, each Sl1∣12,12,α=2⟩\Sl{l}\ka{\h}{2}Sl1​∣21​,21​,α=2⟩ is a Clebsch–Gordan combination of tilde states, and tilde states with different J~\widetilde JJ are orthogonal, so the squared norm of each Sl1∣12,12,α=2⟩\Sl{l}\ka{\h}{2}Sl1​∣21​,21​,α=2⟩ is a sum of squared CG coefficients times the ∥∣J,M~⟩∥2.\big\lVert\lvert\widetilde{J,M}\rangle\big\rVert^2\text{.}​∣J,M​⟩​2. Summing the squared Clebsch–Gordan coefficients over lll gives (2J+1)/(2j+1),(2J+1)/(2j+1)\text{,}(2J+1)/(2j+1), where j=12j=\hj=21​ is the spin of the irrep we started from. That’s 2 for J=32J=\tthJ=23​ and 1 for J=12J=\hJ=21​ (you can confirm it with the table in Section 9). So the sum rule reads

∑l∥Sl1∣j,m⟩∥2=∑J2J+12j+1 ∥∣J,M~⟩∥2,\sum_l\big\lVert\Sl{l}\ket{j,m}\big\rVert^2 = \sum_J \frac{2J+1}{2j+1}\,\big\lVert\lvert\widetilde{J,M}\rangle\big\rVert^2 ,l∑​​Sl1​∣j,m⟩​2=J∑​2j+12J+1​​∣J,M​⟩​2,

1. The other copy

Everything in Step 2 used only the commutators and the action of J−,J_-\text{,}J−​, which are the same for both copies, so eq. (32) holds with α=2\alpha=2α=2 replaced by α=1.\alpha=1\text{.}α=1. ∣32,32~⟩(1)=S+11∣12,12,α=1⟩=−12⋅12 ∣↑↑↑⟩=−12 ∣32,32⟩.\lvert\widetilde{\tth,\tth}\rangle^{(1)} = \Sl{+1}\ka{\h}{1} = -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\,\ket{\U\U\U} = -\tfrac12\,\ket{\tth,\tth}.∣23​,23​​⟩(1)=S+11​∣21​,21​,α=1⟩=−2​1​⋅2​1​∣↑↑↑⟩=−21​∣23​,23​⟩.
(56)

For the other tower we need S01∣12,12,α=1⟩=−122(∣↑↓↑⟩+∣↓↑↑⟩)\Sl{0}\ka{\h}{1} = -\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}\big(\ket{\U\D\U}+ \ket{\D\U\U}\big)S01​∣21​,21​,α=1⟩=−22​1​(∣↑↓↑⟩+∣↓↑↑⟩) and S+11∣12,−12,α=1⟩=−12∣↑↑↓⟩.\Sl{+1}\ka{\mh}{1} = -\tfrac12\ket{\U\U\D}\text{.}S+11​∣21​,−21​,α=1⟩=−21​∣↑↑↓⟩. Then

∣12,12~⟩(1)=−13 S01∣12,12,α=1⟩+23 S+11∣12,−12,α=1⟩=126(∣↑↓↑⟩+∣↓↑↑⟩)−16 ∣↑↑↓⟩=−12 ∣12,12,α=2⟩,\begin{aligned} \lvert\widetilde{\h,\h}\rangle^{(1)} &= -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\,\Sl{0}\ka{\h}{1} + \sqrt{\tfrac23}\,\Sl{+1}\ka{\mh}{1}\\ &= \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt6}\big(\ket{\U\D\U}+\ket{\D\U\U}\big) - \tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}\,\ket{\U\U\D} = -\tfrac12\,\ka{\h}{2}, \end{aligned}∣21​,21​​⟩(1)​=−3​1​S01​∣21​,21​,α=1⟩+32​​S+11​∣21​,−21​,α=1⟩=26​1​(∣↑↓↑⟩+∣↓↑↑⟩)−6​1​∣↑↑↓⟩=−21​∣21​,21​,α=2⟩,​
(57)

by eq. (26). So k1,3/23/2,1/2=−12,k^{3/2,1/2}_{1,3/2}=-\tfrac12\text{,}k1,3/23/2,1/2​=−21​, k1,11/2,1/2=0,k^{1/2,1/2}_{1,1}=0\text{,}k1,11/2,1/2​=0, and k1,21/2,1/2=−12.k^{1/2,1/2}_{1,2}=-\tfrac12\text{.}k1,21/2,1/2​=−21​.

Why the zero? In the α=1\alpha=1α=1 copy, particles 1 and 2 form a singlet, which is annihilated by S(1)+S(2).\vec S^{(1)}+\vec S^{(2)}\text{.}S(1)+S(2). So on these states S(2)\vec S^{(2)}S(2) acts like 12(S(2)−S(1)),\tfrac12\big(\vec S^{(2)}-\vec S^{(1)}\big)\text{,}21​(S(2)−S(1)), which is odd under swapping particles 1 and 2. It turns the (odd) singlet into an (even) triplet, so everything it produces has j12=1.j_{12}=1\text{.}j12​=1. That sector contains the α=2\alpha=2α=2 copy and the spin-32\tth23​ states, but not the α=1\alpha=1α=1 copy.

For the sum rule, both towers have squared norm 14,\tfrac14\text{,}41​, and 2⋅14+1⋅14=34.{2\cdot\tfrac14+1\cdot\tfrac14}=\tfrac34\text{.}2⋅41​+1⋅41​=43​. It works.

Remark: Notice that k1,21/2,1/2=k2,11/2,1/2=−12:k^{1/2,1/2}_{1,2}=k^{1/2,1/2}_{2,1}=-\tfrac12\text{:}k1,21/2,1/2​=k2,11/2,1/2​=−21​: the reduced matrix element from copy 1 to copy 2 equals the one from copy 2 to copy 1. That’s what you’d expect from the Hermiticity of S(2)\vec S^{(2)}S(2) (see the remark at the end of the next solution). ♣\clubsuit♣

Its inner products with ∣12,12,α=1⟩\ka{\h}{1}∣21​,21​,α=1⟩ and ∣12,12,α=2⟩\ka{\h}{2}∣21​,21​,α=2⟩ from eqs. (25) and (26) are

and its inner product with ∣32,12⟩\ket{\tth,\h}∣23​,21​⟩ is zero, as it must be. So

For the sum rule, now with j=32,j=\tth\text{,}j=23​, the weights are (2J+1)/(2j+1),(2J+1)/(2j+1)\text{,}(2J+1)/(2j+1), which are 12,\tfrac12\text{,}21​, 1,1\text{,}1, and 32\tfrac3223​ for J=12,32,52.J=\h,\tth,\fh\text{.}J=21​,23​,25​.
